Across DeepWalk, LINE, and node2vec, the core idea is to reuse the natural language Skip-gram model as a neighborhood-prediction objective for graphs, but each method defines the “context” differently.

DeepWalk adapts the Skip-gram model by first generating short random walks over the graph and then treating each walk like a sentence: nodes appearing within a fixed window on the same walk are treated as context for one another. The model then learns node embeddings that maximize the likelihood of predicting these context nodes from a center node, analogous to word2vec in text.

LINE adapts the same general embedding goal differently: instead of random-walk sentences, it directly preserves graph proximity by optimizing objectives for first-order and second-order proximity. In practice, LINE uses a Skip-gram-like negative-sampling formulation to learn embeddings from observed edges and neighborhood distributions, so the learned vectors capture local graph structure without relying on random walks.

node2vec also uses a Skip-gram objective on random-walk-generated node sequences, but it changes the walk strategy. It introduces biased second-order random walks controlled by return and in-out parameters, allowing the walks to interpolate between breadth-first-search-like exploration and depth-first-search-like exploration. This makes the sampled contexts more flexible, and the Skip-gram model then learns embeddings from those biased walk neighborhoods.

So, in all three papers, Skip-gram is adapted from words to nodes by replacing textual co-occurrence with graph-derived co-occurrence; the main differences are whether the context comes from unbiased random walks (DeepWalk), direct edge/proximity modeling (LINE), or biased random walks with tunable exploration behavior (node2vec).
